sources.title: KDIGO: 2024 CKD Evaluation and Management Guideline
ADA: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026

questions.question: An older adult with vomiting and poor intake has orthostatic symptoms, dry mucosa, rising creatinine, concentrated urine, and no active urine sediment. Which mechanism is most likely?
choices: Reduced renal perfusion lowers GFR while intact tubules conserve sodium and water
Immune-complex glomerulonephritis increases filtration surface area
Established tubular necrosis preserves maximal concentrating ability
Bilateral ureteral obstruction increases effective arterial volume
rationales: Volume depletion produces prerenal physiology; functioning tubules respond by concentrating urine and conserving sodium.
Glomerulonephritis usually creates an active sediment with blood, protein, or casts.
Damaged tubules lose concentrating and sodium-reabsorbing ability.
Obstruction is postrenal and does not explain the volume-depletion findings.
questions.explanation: Prerenal findings reflect a hemodynamic fall in filtration before structural tubular injury; delayed correction can progress to ischemic tubular damage.

questions.question: After prolonged hypotension, a patient remains oliguric despite restoration of circulation. Urine microscopy shows muddy brown granular casts. Which lesion is most likely?
choices: Acute tubular injury with sloughed epithelial cells and impaired tubular function
Minimal-change nephrotic syndrome
Isolated renal-artery vasospasm with completely intact tubules
Lower urinary-tract infection confined to the bladder
rationales: Muddy brown granular casts are strongly associated with acute tubular injury/necrosis after ischemic or toxic damage.
Minimal-change disease causes heavy proteinuria without this sediment pattern.
Persistent casts indicate structural tubular injury rather than purely reversible hemodynamics.
Cystitis does not produce renal tubular casts.
questions.explanation: The transition from prerenal physiology to structural tubular injury changes the expected urine sediment and recovery pattern.

questions.question: A patient develops edema, hypertension, hematuria, and reduced kidney function two weeks after an infection. Urine microscopy shows dysmorphic red cells and red-cell casts. Where is the primary lesion?
choices: Glomerular capillaries
Renal pelvis only
Proximal tubules only
Bladder mucosa
rationales: Dysmorphic red cells and red-cell casts localize bleeding to the glomerulus and nephron.
Pelvic bleeding does not typically create red-cell casts.
Tubular injury more often produces epithelial or granular casts.
Bladder bleeding occurs downstream and cannot form casts within renal tubules.
questions.explanation: Urine microscopy can anatomically localize disease; casts form in tubules and therefore point above the lower urinary tract.

questions.question: A patient has heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, edema, and hyperlipidemia. Which additional risk follows directly from urinary loss of anticoagulant proteins and increased hepatic procoagulant synthesis?
choices: Venous thrombosis
Severe neutropenia
Respiratory alkalosis from bicarbonate retention
Universal gross hematuria
rationales: Nephrotic syndrome creates a hypercoagulable state through urinary anticoagulant loss and altered hepatic protein synthesis.
Neutrophil number is not predictably depleted by this mechanism.
The coagulation changes do not cause the described acid-base disorder.
Gross hematuria is not universal and is more suggestive of a nephritic or urologic process.
questions.explanation: Nephrotic syndrome is systemic: protein loss contributes not only to edema but also thrombosis and infection risk.

questions.question: A patient with benign prostatic enlargement develops anuria, suprapubic discomfort, and a distended bladder. What is the immediate pathophysiologic concern?
choices: Postrenal obstruction raises pressure upstream and can rapidly reduce GFR
Low plasma oncotic pressure is pulling filtrate back into glomeruli
Excess erythropoietin is blocking urine formation
Isolated distal tubular acidosis is closing the urethra
rationales: Outflow obstruction transmits pressure proximally and lowers net filtration; prompt assessment and relief are important.
Oncotic pressure does not explain a distended bladder and acute anuria.
Erythropoietin does not obstruct urinary flow.
Tubular acid handling does not mechanically close the urethra.
questions.explanation: Postrenal AKI may be reversible when obstruction is identified and relieved promptly, so bladder and collecting-system assessment is time sensitive.

questions.question: A patient with kidney failure has potassium 7.1 mEq/L, weakness, and widening of the QRS complex. Which treatment priority is most immediate?
choices: Stabilize the cardiac membrane while urgently lowering and removing potassium
Wait for a repeat outpatient level because total-body potassium is always low
Give potassium supplementation to correct intracellular depletion
Treat only the serum creatinine because ECG changes are unrelated
rationales: Severe hyperkalemia with ECG changes is life threatening; immediate membrane stabilization and rapid potassium-shifting/removal strategies are required.
The ECG abnormality confirms immediate risk and should not be managed as routine follow-up.
Additional potassium could worsen fatal arrhythmia risk.
Hyperkalemia directly alters cardiac conduction and must be treated independently of the creatinine number.
questions.explanation: Advanced prioritization separates three goals: protect the myocardium, shift potassium intracellularly, and remove potassium from the body.

questions.question: A patient with diarrhea has pH 7.29, bicarbonate 15 mEq/L, and PaCO2 30 mm Hg. Which interpretation is best?
choices: Primary metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation that is approximately appropriate
Primary respiratory acidosis with renal bicarbonate loss as compensation
Primary metabolic alkalosis with hypoventilation
Normal acid-base status because PaCO2 is within some laboratory reference ranges
rationales: Low pH and bicarbonate identify metabolic acidosis; a PaCO2 near the expected Winter-formula range suggests appropriate compensation.
Respiratory acidosis would have an elevated primary PaCO2.
Metabolic alkalosis requires elevated bicarbonate.
Values must be interpreted together rather than separately against reference ranges.
questions.explanation: Checking expected compensation helps detect a second acid-base disorder instead of assuming every abnormal PaCO2 is compensatory.

questions.question: A patient has one eGFR value of 52 mL/min/1.73 m² during an acute illness. Which statement about chronic kidney disease is most accurate?
choices: One abnormal value does not establish chronicity; repeat assessment and markers of kidney damage over at least three months are needed
Any eGFR below 60 for one day proves permanent CKD
Albuminuria is irrelevant when eGFR exceeds 30
CKD classification uses serum creatinine alone and never urine findings
rationales: CKD requires abnormalities of kidney structure or function present for at least three months; acute changes must be distinguished.
A transient AKI can lower eGFR without proving chronic disease.
Albuminuria materially affects CKD category and risk even at higher eGFR.
Current classification combines cause, GFR category, and albuminuria category.
questions.explanation: Correct labeling prevents an acute illness from being misclassified as chronic while still ensuring timely reassessment.

questions.question: A volume-depleted patient taking an ACE inhibitor begins frequent NSAID use and develops acute kidney injury. Which combined arteriolar effects reduce glomerular filtration pressure?
choices: NSAID-related afferent constriction plus ACE-inhibitor–related efferent dilation
Afferent dilation plus efferent constriction
Dilation of both arterioles with increased filtration pressure
Constriction of both ureters from prostaglandin excess
rationales: Renal prostaglandins support afferent dilation during low perfusion; NSAIDs remove that support, while ACE inhibition reduces efferent constriction.
This combination would tend to support or raise intraglomerular pressure rather than explain the injury.
The actual drug effects are not dilation of both arterioles.
These medications alter renal hemodynamics, not ureteral smooth muscle through prostaglandin excess.
questions.explanation: The interaction becomes especially hazardous when effective circulating volume is low because both compensatory ends of the glomerulus are impaired.

questions.question: A patient with chronic severe hyponatremia develops confusion but no seizure. Why must correction be carefully controlled even when treatment is needed?
choices: Overly rapid sodium rise can cause osmotic demyelination after brain adaptation to chronic hypo-osmolality
Slow correction causes immediate cerebral salt crystallization
Chronic hyponatremia prevents any change in brain-cell osmolytes
Rapid correction is harmless if serum creatinine is normal
rationales: Brain cells adapt to chronic hypo-osmolality by losing osmolytes; rapid extracellular tonicity increase can injure oligodendrocytes and cause osmotic demyelination.
Salt crystallization is not the mechanism.
Osmolyte adaptation is precisely why chronicity affects correction risk.
Normal creatinine does not remove the neurologic risk of overly rapid correction.
questions.explanation: Hyponatremia management balances the danger of cerebral edema from low sodium against demyelination from excessive correction; severity and chronicity guide monitored treatment.
